Effects of Interior Color Schemes on
Emotion, Task Performance, and Heart
Rate in Immersive Virtual Environments
SeungHyunCha,Ph.D. ,HanyangUniversity,RepublicofKorea
ShaojieZhang,M.S.,TheHongKongPolytechnicUniversity,HongKong
TaeWanKim,Ph.D. ,IncheonNationalUniversity,RepublicofKorea
ABSTRACT
The purpose of this study was to investigate the effects of interior color schemes in immersive
virtual environments (IVEs) on emotion, task performance, and heart rate to examine IVEs’
potential for interior color research. Fifty-five (n = 55) student participants were recruited to
experience four different colored IVE models (i.e., red, green, blue, and white), and their emo-
tions, heart rate change, and proofreading performances during the immersion were measured.
Participants were also asked about their sense of presence after the experience. The findings
support the following three hypotheses: (1) IVE interior color schemes affect subject emotion,
(2) IVE interior color schemes affect subject task performance as measured through a proofread-
ingexercise,and(3)IVEinteriorcolorschemesaffectsubjectheartrate.Specifically,redwasper-
ceived as significantly heavier, warmer, more exciting, tenser, and unpleasant. Significantly
fewer errors occurred during the white immersion versus the green color scheme when complet-
ing the task performance exercise. While heart rate was reduced for each color, significant
decreases were detected in the blue, white, and green color scenarios. The majority of partici-
pants felt a sense of being there when experiencing the four colored IVE spaces. Based on these
results,weconcludethatIVEhaspotentialforinteriorcolorresearch toovercomethelimitations
oftraditionalcolorresearchtools.
INTRODUCTION
Visual comfort, defined as the subjective impression of an individual’s comfort caused by the
visual environment (Davis & Nutter, 2010), is important for building users’ well-being and pro-
ductivity. A visual environment is characterized by several parameters, including interior color,
spatialfeatures, andmaterial textures;inparticular, interiorcolor playsanimportant role infor-
ming users’ sense of visual comfort aesthetically, indicatively, and symbolically (Al et al., 2016).
Inorder toknowhowusers’emotion,physiologicalresponse,satisfaction, andtask performance
change in response to different colors, studies have manipulated interior colors in physical
spaces (e.g., laboratory and real-life spaces) and measured the impacts on building users
(Al-Ayash, Kane, Smith, & Green-Armytage, 2016; Küller, Mikellides, & Janssens, 2009; Yildirim,
Akalin-Baskaya, & Hidayetoglu, 2007; Yildirim, Capanoglu, Cagatay, & Hidayetoglu, 2012).
Despitethebenefitsrealphysical spaces canbringtoresearch,thisapproachexhibitslimitations
in controllability and cost-effectiveness. For example, changing interior color properties
(i.e., hue, value, and saturation) and controlling other confounding settings is difficult to realize
in a physical space. In addition, mockups with different interior colors must be constructed to
satisfyeachexperimentalrequirement,whichcanbetime-consumingandexpensive.
Thus, visual display tools (such as two-dimensional [2D] visual displays and three-dimensional
[3D] nonimmersive visual displays on desktop computers) have been gradually adopted in inte-

utilized 3D nonimmersive visual displays in exploring changes in emotional response (Naz,
Kopper, McMahan, & Nadin, 2017) and wayfinding performance (Hidayetoglu, Yildirim, &
Akalin, 2012) according to different interior colors. However, these visual display tools often
lack certain visual cues (e.g., depth perception and spatial orientation), do not allow one-to-
one scale, and fail to isolate users from the surrounding environment. Such shortcomings of
visual display tools can affect the results of interior color studies because they may distort
users’ perception of context and sense of presence (i.e., the feeling that you are “there”). As a
matter of fact, context is among the most important source of colors’ psychological meaning, a
notion known as color-in-context theory (Elliot & Maier, 2012). Due to changes of color mean-
ing in unrepresentative contexts, users are likely to have confounding responses to different
interior colors. In addition, a low degree of presence has a negative impact on ecological valid-
ity (i.e., a measure of how a test predicts behaviors in real-world settings) (Deniaud, Honnet,
Jeanne, & Mestre, 2015), which reduces the generalizability of findings concerning interior
color.
In this context, immersive virtual environment (IVE) has gained increasing interest because it
can provide virtual spaces for interior color experiments with full one-to-one modeling and 3D
visualization technologies that allow users to view and interact in real time from a first-person
perspective that promotes their spatial perception and sense of presence (Niu, Pan, &
Zhao, 2016). A cross-sectional study also emphasized that IVEs can offer more ecological validity
compared with computer graphics with the same experimental control (Loomis, Blascovich, &
Beall, 1999). Despite some studies that demonstrate the similarity between IVEs and real physi-
cal spaces in terms of architectural appearances (e.g., height and size) (Cha, Koo, Kim, &
Hong, 2019), sense of presence and user responses (Heydarian et al., 2015; Kuliga, Thrash, Dal-
ton, & Hölscher, 2015; Westerdahl et al., 2006) to different interior colors have not been exam-
ined for testing the feasibility of IVEs for use in interior color

(Al-Ayash et al., 2016; Kwallek, Woodson, Lewis, & Sales, 1997) have investigated user
responses—focusing on emotion, task performance, or heart rate change—to different colors
and found relationships between user perception and colors. Birren (2006) points out that
colors have a strong impact on emotions such as feeling strong, weak, warm, or calm. Task and
heart rate are also affected by interior color schemes (Al-Ayash et al., 2016; Kwallek, Soon, &
Lewis, 2007). Abbas, Kumar, and Mclachlan (2005) found that red increased subjects’ heart rate,
while blue decreased it. Kwallek, Lewis, Lin-Hsiao, and Woodson (1996) found that subjects
made significantly more errors in the white color scheme than in the red or blue schemes.
Based on these findings, we developed the following hypotheses regarding user responses to
interior color schemes in IVEs and compared results to previous color studies to determine if
IVEs can be a reliable simulation tool. While color research is robust using real-life settings, IVE
has not been investigated extensively. Because of this lack of IVE literature, we opted to use
nondirectional hypothesestesting.

LITERATURE REVIEW
Thissectionreviewstheliteratureontherelationshipbetweeninteriorcolorsandpeople’semo-
tion, task performance, and heart rate to illustrate the variety of case-specific color studies in
diverse contexts. Moreover, IVE’s technical advantages and practical applications are discussed
as a method for representing interior colors, compared to physical spaces and certain visual
computerdisplaytools.
INTERIOR COLORS AFFECT EMOTION, TASK PERFORMANCE, AND HEART RATE
It is generally believed that color affects human emotion, task performance, and heart rate,
although some studies offer contradictory results. First, color is often used to describe diverse
emotions such as green for envy, red for rage, and blue for depression (Carruthers, Morris,
Tarrier, & Whorwell, 2010). Representatively, it is well-known that warm colors such as red and
yellow are more stimulating and arousing, whereas cool colors such as blue and green are
calming (Greene, Bell, & Boyer, 1983; Kurt & Osueke, 2014; Kwallek et al., 2007; Wexner, 1954).
ClarkeandCostall(2008)supportthisideaintheirsemistructuredinterviewswithuniversitystu-
dents (n = 16), claiming that blue, green, and violet are regarded as cool, calming, and relaxing
and can soothe anxiety levels. Red and yellow are seen as warm and exciting and can increase
arousal levels. Al-Ayash et al. (2016) assessed university students’ (n = 24) emotion using eight
adjective pairs (e.g., pleasant/unpleasant, dark/light, etc.) in a test room in which color was dif-
ferentiated using hanging panels. According to the study results, blue instigated more positive
emotions—pleasant, relaxing, and calming—than red and yellow. Yildirim et al. (2007) investi-
gated emotions of customers (n = 245) in a café/restaurant by manipulating interior wall color
using yellow and violet. They found that yellow interior walls were perceived as roomier, more
pleasant, and more interesting. Kwallek and Lewis (1990) (n = 222), in their seminal work, con-
ducted an experiment to assess mood using a questionnaire in three office environments with
different colors—red, green, and white. The subjects displayed more tension in the red office.
Kwallek et al. (1997) (n = 90) reported similar results where red offices caused more tension to
subjects than blue or green offices. On the other hand, Ainsworth, Simpson, and Cassell (1993)
(n = 45) found no significant relationships between colors and mood in a red, blue–green, and
white office environment. Research by Kwallek et al. (1996) supports this claim by finding no
overall main effects of office colors on mood. Clearly, color

needed.

Heart rate, a physiological state of people, can also be affected by interior color schemes and
exposure time to a color. Abbas et al. (2005) measured heart rates of voluntary subjects (most
were university students; n = 15) after showing them different colored lights for 8 minutes and
found that red (i.e., arousing) increased subjects’ heart rates, while blue (i.e., calming)
decreased it. In Al-Ayash et al.’s (2016) study, red and yellow color schemes led to increased
heart rates, while blue led to decreased heart rates after university students (n = 24) were
exposedfor5minutes.Theseresultsimplythatcolorswitharousingpropertiesstimulatepeople
and increase their heart rate. However, heart rates of university students (n = 60) exposed for
1 minute to color schemes did not appear to be significantly impacted (Caldwell & Jones, 1985).
If the exposure time is too short, people will not wholly immerse themselves in the color
scheme, and the experiment will not reveal the relationship between color schemes and heart
rate(Kueller&Mikellides,1993).
Thecontradictory results inthe literature arenotsurprising asmany studiesnotethe difficulties
of generalization of color research over diverse participants (Manav, 2006; Saito, 1996). Indeed,
Clarke and Costall (2008) claim that meanings of colors originate from individual experience,
affected by the surrounding environment such as media and education. According to
Schirillo (2001), humans’ perception of colors can be differentiated by cultural and geographical
proximity. For example, white in Asian regions is generally preferred due to its positive associa-
tions with cleanliness, purity, and refreshing qualities (Saito, 1996). Age and gender can also be
factors that affect color perception (Manav, 2006). Varying results of color studies demand the
needforcase-specificcolorresearchthatcanbeuseddiversely.

However, a 3D nonimmersive visual display does not let users experience a one-to-one scale

model, which could isolate them from the surrounding environment. A study by Deniaud
etal.(2015)indicated thatsuch alowsense ofpresence reduces ecological validity, whichlimits

An IVE has numerous advantages in visualizing interior color compared to computer-generated
images and nonimmersive virtual environments (VE). First, evidence suggests that the one-to-
one scale model offered by IVEs can give users more accurate spatial perceptions (Linzer, Mar-
tens, & Voigt, 1994). They can, thus, better understand interior color in specific contexts, which
promotes a realistic perception that mimics the real world. Second, users are enveloped within
IVEs by a Head-Mounted Display (HMD) that isolates them from the visual stimuli in their sur-
rounding environment. Confounding effects on participants’ responses (e.g., lighting quality) can
be eliminated. Moreover, some cross-sectional studies demonstrated that users identify objec-
tives more accurately and feel like they are “there” within IVEs, compared with nonimmersive
VEs (North & North, 2016; Paes, Arantes, & Irizarry, 2017). IVE with an immersive visual display
has also been identified as affording a higher degree of ecological validity with the same experi-
mental control compared to a computer graphic display (Loomis et al., 1999). Thus, research
findingscapturedusingIVEsaremorelikelytobegeneralizabletoreal-lifesituations.
To be useful as a display for color studies, IVEs must offer users a realistic or naturalistic experi-
ence. Interest in examining whether IVE offers such an experience dramatically increased, as
seen in the commonplace application in many fields. Architectural studies have reported that
IVEs are able to realistically represent spaces to a fair extent, based on the similarity of behav-
ioral outcomes (e.g., navigation) and subjective assessment (e.g., environmental description and
sense of presence). To achieve the long-term goal of exploring lighting-related behavior via IVE,
Heydarian et al. (2015) conducted a benchmark study which indicated that users (n = 120) felt a
strong sense of presence within two basic lighting conditions (dark and light) simulated by IVEs.
In addition, similar task performance was found to occur in IVEs and the corresponding physical
offices for two tasks (a writing task and a matching task). In the field of urban planning, a cross-
sectional study identified congruence in acoustic and visual stimuli between IVEs and the
corresponding real-life urban environments by assessing subjective ratings (Maffei, Masullo,
Pascale, Ruggiero, & Romero, 2016). Similarly, another study

METHODOLOGY
The objective of this study was to investigate effects of interior color schemes in IVEs on emo-
tion, task performance, heart rate, and sense of presence to examine their potential for use in
interior color research. It iscrucial that IVE models, apparatus, questionnaires, and experimental
procedures are adequate for the experimental design. This study adopted best practices from
IVE and color-related studies (Al-Ayash et al., 2016; Heydarian et al., 2015; Heydarian & Becerik-
Gerber,2017;Külleretal.,2009)tooptimizetheresearchmethodology.
EXPERIMENTAL SETTINGS
The context of this study (e.g., space type, variables of interests, and preparatory work) was
determined to eliminate experimental mishaps. The variables of interest solely focused on the
hue of the interior color, and other attributes (e.g., value and saturation) were well controlled
at an equivalent degree. Several color studies have focused on red, white, blue, and green (Al-
Ayash et al., 2016; Kwallek et al., 2005). Referring to a cross-sectional study related to interior
color (Kwallek et al., 1996), color samples in this study were chosen as 6.05R 4.59/11.15 (red),
9.75YR 8.74/0.45 (white), 3.45G 4.44/7.89 (green), and 2.43PB 5.12/10.51 (blue). Emotion was
measured using a questionnaire with eight bipolar adjectives on a 1–7 semantic scale
(i.e., Heavy/Light, Calm/Exciting, Weak/Strong, Cool/Warm, Tense/Relax, Unpleasant/Pleasant,
JOURNALOFINTERIORDESIGN 55

Interesting/Boring, and Dark/Light) selected from the Color Image Scale (Kobayashi, 1981). To
indicate effects of interior colors on physiological change, heart rate data were collected during
normal conditions and during the experimental session using Polar H7, a real-time heart rate
sensor. To measure task performance, previous studies used various types of tests, such as the
SAT reading comprehension (Al-Ayash et al., 2016), Minnesota Clerical Test (Kwallek
et al., 1996), and math problems (Stone, 2001). Like Kwallek et al. (2007), we used a proofread-
ing task to measure task performance among the different interior color schemes. As itis a vital
indicator to show the effectiveness of IVEs, sense of presence was measured through an IVE
experience survey (Igroup Presence Questionnaire [IPQ]). The IPQ consists of four groups of
questions: general “sense of being there,” spatial presence, involvement, and experience real-
ism. A simplified IPQ was adopted involving five questions using a 5-point Likert scale
(1=stronglydisagreeand5=strongly agree),whichmainlyfocused onthesense ofbeingphys-
icallypresentintheIVE(Schubert,Friedmann, &Regenbrecht,2001).
Preparatory work was required to identify and eliminate extraneous effects on study outcomes.
Apartfrominteriorcolor,lightinglevelalsosignificantlyimpactedusers’sensationofvisualcom-
fort (Bellia, Bisegna, & Spada, 2011; Durak, Olguntürk, Yener, Güvenç, & Gürçinar, 2007). Thus,
the lighting level was kept at 500lx, which is recommended for office-related activity, while the
interior colors were manipulated in four IVE models. To eliminate the effects of other con-
founding factors on physiological responses, indoor temperature was controlled at 23(cid:1)C, and
participants were not allowed to engage in strenuous physical activities. In addition, some real-
life objects were embedded in the IVE models, such as carpeting, acoustical ceiling tile, texture,
anddoors.

PARTICIPANTS
Fifty-five (n = 55) participants were recruited through flyers on the campus of the Hong Kong
Polytechnic University. A gift coupon was given for their participation. Subjects were Asian,
20–28years old (M =21.34, SD =1.44),with 7 females and 48 males. Forty-nine were engineer-
ingstudents;thereststudiedothermajorssuchasmanagementandeducation.

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE
Prior to commencing the main experiment, participants were prepared for the study (Figure 3).
First, they completed the Ishihara Color Blindness Test, and those who passed were allowed to
continue with the rest of the experiment. Before signing a consent form, they were informed
about potential risks of IVE-based experiments. Participants were trained in navigating within
the IVE. Following the training session, participants were equipped with the Polar H7 that mea-
suresreal-timeheartrate(Figure3).
Once this preparatory work was done,the experiment began. The researcher helped the partici-
pant adjust to the Oculus Rift until he or she felt comfortable in the virtual space. Participants
were randomly assigned to one of four color schemes to eliminate the order effect. The Polar
H7 was set to measure their current heart rate while they were experiencing a color scheme in
the IVE for 2 minutes. Participants then performed the proofreading task as accurately as possi-
ble. The number of proofreading errors was recorded, and the amount of time each participant
spentonthetaskwasmeasuredusingastopwatch.
Upon completing the proofreading task, participants were asked to remove the HMD to reduce
motion sickness and then complete a questionnaire about color-related emotion. There was a
5-minute rest period between experimental sessions to eliminate any carryover effect. During
the rest period, participants’ heart rates were recorded as baseline data to compare to heart
rates recorded in the experimental sessions. The same experimental procedure was repeated
for the remaining three color schemes in a random order. Once participants had experienced all
fourcolorschemes,theycompletedthesenseofpresence questionnaire (Figure3).
DATA ANALYSIS
In this study, proofreading performance was measured as the number of errors per minute,
ratherthansimplythenumberoferrors,becausetimespentonthetaskcouldaffecttheperfor-
mance. In addition, data retrieved from the questionnaires used the same response scale to
avoid coding errors or missing data. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was utilized to com-
paremeansofdatasamples(white,red,green, andblue inthisstudy). Toanalyze thechange in
heart rate between the baseline and experimental conditions, a paired-sample t-test was used
toanalyzepaireddataacrossdifferentmeasures.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
The primary statistical procedures used to analyze the measured data were one-way ANOVA
and a paired-sample t-test. The results were analyzed with reference to previous findings of

Notably, no significant difference was found for Interesting/Boring, which is inconsistent with
previous findings (Al-Ayash et al., 2016; Yildirim et al., 2007). Yildirim et al. studied the relation-
ship between store atmospheric attributes and interior colors (i.e., yellow and violet) and found
that Interesting/Boring is among the most influenced emotions by color. Al-Ayash et al. also
indicate that hue has an impact on Interesting/Boring, although no effect of value was found.
This difference could be explained by the fact that the IVE experience of wearing a VR headset
is already interesting, so perhaps participants are not bored by IVE experiences that use four
color schemes. It should also be noted that different contexts and colors were used for these
studies. Yildirim et al. examined customers’ emotion in an actual café/restaurant using yellow
andviolet.Al-Ayash et al. conducted their experimentsina testroom usinghanging panels with
different colors. These context differences could also explain diverse users’ emotion as
supportedbycolor-in-contexttheory(Elliot&Maier,2012).
Post-hoc comparisons using Tukey’s Honest Significant Difference (HSD) test indicated that red
was rated significantly more exciting, stronger, warmer, and tenser than the three other colors,
with a p-value less than .001 in all comparisons. These results support the prevailing perception
of the impact of color on emotion (Birren, 2006; Kwallek et al., 2007; Ou, Luo, Woodcock, &
Wright, 2004). For example, Al-Ayash et al. (2016) pointed out that red is more stimulating,
whereas white and green are calming. Similarly, Clarke and Costall (2008) indicate that blue and
green colors are perceived as cool, relaxing, and calming, whereas red is seen as warm and
arousing.KurtandOsueke(2014,p.4)claimthatpsychologicalconnotationsofredarepowerful
andstrong,and Pamukand Göknar(2010)offered adefinitionofredwiththe words“I’mfiery.”
“I’mstrong.”Ourresultssupportthisliterature.
In Tukey’s HSD test, red was perceived the heaviest compared to blue (p = .001), green
(p<.001), and white (p<.001). Similarly, red was seen as the heaviest compared to other
colors in Al-Ayash et al.’s (2016) study. On the other hand, white was perceived to be the

HEART RATE CHANGE
Heart rates were measured in the resting zone as baseline data (i.e., initial heart rates) and again
during each experimental session (i.e., affected heart rates). Measured heart rate data were ana-
lyzed using paired-samples t-tests. Surprisingly, for all color schemes, heart rates of subjects
decreased after they were immersed in the IVE spaces. Significant decreases in heart rates were
detected in blue (t(54) = 3.414, p = .001), white (t(54) = 2.390, p = .021), and green (t(54) = 2.404,
p = .020) color schemes. Although there were some decreases in heart rates in the red color
scheme,theamountofdecreaseswasthesmallestamongthefourcolorschemes,andthisdecrease
was not statistically significant (t(54) = 1.816, p = .076) at the set confidence level. These findings
supporthypothesisH3(IVEinteriorcolorschemeswillaffectsubjectheartrate)(Figure6).
These findings are well aligned with studies (Abbas et al., 2005; Al-Ayash et al., 2016) which
state that blue is calming and decreases heart rates of people when they are exposed to this

SENSE OF PRESENCE
For the IPQ, the majority of participants felt present when experiencing the four colored IVE
spaces (Table 1). Around 70% of participants (n = 38) had a sense of being there, while 80%
(n = 46) felt that the virtual space was around them. Having participants complete the proof-
reading task while in the IVE may have led to a high sense of being there and feeling sur-
rounded by the virtual space. Moreover, these IVE models contained real-life features such as
texture, ceiling tiles, and doors that enriched the vividness. Such features perhaps increase the
sense of a real-world space, giving participants the perception of an actual interior. These find-
ings support the literature stating that IVEs have the ability to give users more accurate spatial
perception, realistic insights, and may be generalizable to real-life situations (Linzer et al., 1994;
North&North,2016;Paesetal.,2017).
However, participants gave an average rating for sense of acting in the IVE space (M = 3.40),
and some participants perceived the four colored IVE spaces as being similar to pictures
(M = 3.17). The reason might be that a lack of dynamic movement and interaction with IVE
spaces makes them seem static. Indeed, Heydarian et al. (2015) provided interaction functions
such as crouching, grabbing, and moving objects in their IVE experiments, thus increasing the
realismofinteracting andbeinginthespace.Futurestudiesshouldexamine theideaofworking
orcompletingvarioustasksintheIVE.
CONCLUSIONS
Extensive research regarding interior colors has been conducted in physical spaces (Al-Ayash
et al., 2016; Küller et al., 2009; Yildirim et al., 2007). To reduce the effort involved in physically
manipulating interior colors, 2D visual display and 3D nonimmersive visual display have been
JOURNALOFINTERIORDESIGN 61

gradually adopted to generate diverse design alternatives for interior color (Naz et al., 2017; War-
dono et al., 2012; Yildirim et al., 2011). However, they impair the accuracy of user’s responses to
interior color due to technical limitations. As a novel technology, IVE provides several advances
(e.g., immersive display) in visualizing interior colors. Although some studies in other fields
(e.g., architecture and interior lighting) suggest that IVEs can adequately represent physical space
such as height and size (Cha et al., 2019), interior color has not been extensively tested. To bridge
this gap, this study conducted an IVE-based experiment to collect user responses on emotion, heart
ratechange,proofreadingperformance,andsenseofpresenceforfourinteriorcolorschemes.

LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
Despite the technical advantages of applying IVEs in interior color studies, in tandem with the
abilitytosimulateinteriorcolorsastheyappearinrealspaces,thereareseveralissuesthatinte-
rior color researchers should consider during experiments using IVEs. First, because wearing a
HMD can make participants feel uncomfortable or dizzy, IVEs might not be suitable for studies
where participant behavior needs to be observed and measured for longer periods of time. Sec-
ond, participants were observed while using IVE tools, which may make them conscious of the
researchers perhaps more than in traditional experiments and could have been affected less by
colors due to the Hawthorn effect. Third, three of our environments used highly saturated
colors that may not reflect real-world interior spaces. Therefore, to support a wider range of
applicableinteriorcolorresearch,IVEsshouldevolvetoprovidebettercolorrepresentability.
Although this study involved 55 participants in the experiment and conducted statistical
analyses, several additional limitations should be addressed with future research. Most partici-
pants were local college students, which makes our findings difficult to apply to other represen-
tative populations (e.g., employees, people who are older). Additional IVE experiments can be
conducted in the future with other populations, particularly because age can be a variable that
affects color perception (Manav, 2006). Because some participants were nearsighted, they per-
ceivedallIVEmodels asblurry through theHMD,whichmightplayanegativerole indecreasing
sense of presence and precise perception of colored spaces. Finally, only three measures
(i.e.,emotion,heartrate,andproofreading performance)wereusedasindicatorsofuserexperi-
ence. Thus, findings from this study cannot be generalized to other indicators
(e.g., environmental satisfaction, cognitive performance) that reflect interior colors’influence on
users. These aspects of user responses can also be measured and tested with future IVE-based
experiments. Finally, all participants were Asian, and as noted in the literature review, human
perceptiontocolorcanvarybycultureandgeographical proximity(Schirillo,2001).
This research contributes to interior color studies by providing experimental results on the rela-
tionship between colors and emotion, heart rate, and task performance using IVEs. Upon
deployment of IVEs in interior color studies, researchers could use them more frequently
to accumulate knowledge about the impact of colors on users with better controllability and
cost-effectiveness. This research could also enable interior designers to change various colors in
